Weighing two approaches: an "above the clouds" summit look where the stage floats above a sea of clouds with distant peaks poking through, versus a deep valley with mist pooling at the bottom. The clouds-above approach feels cleaner and more dramatic, so I'm leaning toward placing a distant viaduct between two peaks rising above the cloud sea to keep the train sightline visible.

I'm also thinking a small lit mountain hamlet on a ridge above the clouds could give the needed liveliness, with partial gaps in the cloud sea to hint at darker depths below without exposing everything, keeping the kill plane just above the cloud top.

Now I'm composing the distant backdrop around the camera's default north-facing view: a hero peak rising far north from the clouds, catching warm alpenglow on its west face from the setting sun while its east side sits in cool shadow, with other ridgelines framing it to the northwest.

To the northwest I'm placing a curved viaduct carrying the ambient train between rocky shoulders, with a tunnel mouth at one end, set roughly 120-150 units away. The northeast ridge gets a small lit mountain hamlet with pines and drifting snow, while the southern view shows more peaks under the afterglow where the sun just dropped behind the western range, the west sky glowing orange with silhouetted dark-blue peaks, and the east fading to deep violet with early stars and pink-tinged summits. Closer in, around 35-60 units out, I'm scattering rocky spires breaking through the cloud layer to add depth.

I'm adding snowy pines across the nearer spires and the hamlet ridge, and treating the stage's own platform and train pillars as one massif split by a central cleft, merging into a wider base that vanishes into cloud below. The eastern pillar becomes "Portal Rock," rising above the train track with a snow cap and a stone tunnel arch on its west face, possibly marked with a sign — though I need to check that the sign would only be seen at a grazing angle from the default south-facing camera, since the portal faces west.

Repositioning the sign to the rock's south face, facing the platform, makes more sense for visibility from the default view. I'm also weighing whether a station building carved into the platform pillar's south face is worth including, since from the default camera angle it would be mostly hidden below and behind the viewer.

I'm leaning toward skipping a freestanding station house and instead carving a simple facade into Portal Rock's south face — a door, lit windows, the "LAST STOP" sign, and maybe a clock — since that face is directly visible from the platform without adding any obstructive protrusions.

So Portal Rock becomes "the station house rock" overall: tunnel portal on the west face, station facade on the south face, snowy flat top without railings since they'd be obstructive. For the chimney, I'll skip putting it on top to avoid collision issues and instead place it flush on the rock's north face lower down, letting the smoke rise naturally along the rock surface.

For the platform pillar's south side, I'll keep it simple with icicle and snow-ledge detailing rather than adding another window feature. Lighting-wise, I'm planning warm lamps on the station facade to light the east end, the loco headlamp illuminating the buffer stop to the west, and relying on ambient/key lighting plus train window glow rather than adding bollard-mounted platform lamps.

For the platform floor itself, I'm thinking concrete slabs with a yellow safety line and "MIND THE GAP" text near the gap edge, flush snow patches instead of piles so nothing reads as a collision obstacle, tactile paving, manhole covers, and drainage grates for texture, plus a small nameboard -- keeping furniture minimal and avoiding freestanding props like trolleys that would awkwardly double as obstacles.

Looking at other stages' house style confirms this: Splash Deck, Table Manners, and Log Off all keep their primary surfaces clean, so I'll stick with a clear floor and put the richness into the surface treatment instead. The hero element is the train itself -- I'm considering a steam saddle-tank locomotive in a classic mountain railway livery, like red with cream windows reminiscent of the Glacier Express, or dark green with brass and gold lettering.

Red against white snow at dusk would give strong contrast, and I want the roof covered in snow since it's a gameplay surface where dark-colored fighters need to stay readable. For the carriages, I'm adding emissive windows, doors, gangway bellows, visible bogies and wheels, and lettering like "LAST STOP EXPRESS" on a destination board, plus lanterns at the ends. The locomotive gets a red-and-black saddle tank, brass dome, flared chimney, headlamp, buffers, and a lit cab window, skipping the cowcatcher since Swiss-style locos don't typically have one.

Steam rises from the chimney with occasional whistle bursts and low cylinder drain hisses, while the buffer stop at the end of the line gets a glowing red lamp — an iconic detail. The tunnel portal is stone masonry with a keystone and icicles, and I'm layering falling snow particles, flat white caps on roofs, drifts on ledges, and a cloud-sea plane with soft billboard puffs for atmosphere.

Now I'm designing the sky dome as an inverted sphere with a gradient texture shifting from orange-pink at the horizon to deep blue overhead to violet with stars in the east, plus a pale rising moon. For the distant mountains, I'm planning low-poly peaks built in Blender from displaced grids with procedural noise, using slope and height to drive snow-versus-rock coloring.

I'm also laying out other scene elements: a curved multi-arch stone viaduct between cliffs with tunnel portals so the ambient train naturally appears and vanishes, and a hamlet of chalets with lit windows and smoking chimneys nestled above the clouds among pines. Given how much art this entails, I need to prioritize what to build first.

My order will be: the main shell geometry (platform, pillars, train, rock, portal, facade, buffer stop), then sky/clouds/lighting, distant mountain layers, the viaduct with its train, the hamlet and pines, snow/steam/smoke particles, and finally finishing details.

For the gray-box pass, I'm planning to build it procedurally in Unity rather than Blender, focusing on the key masses: the six collision shells, train carriage bodies with bogies and loco details, and base pillar geometry.

I'm also sketching out the cloud sea plane, distant peak cones, viaduct arches, spires, and hamlet ridge, plus one placeholder light — then moving to design-capture and orbit-capture to show the user. I'm weighing whether a gray-box pass is worth the extra step versus jumping straight to art, but since the process calls for gray-box plus human review before locking decisions, I'll keep it fast and lightweight to respect the user's momentum while still asking for a LOCK on the numbered choices.

I'm also working out the camera-yaw convention for the design brief — noticing that Log Off's stated convention (yaw 0° = camera on +Z looking south) doesn't actually match what the design-capture code computes (yaw 0° puts the camera at −Z looking north) — so I'll just define my own clear convention in the brief rather than rely on their possibly-inconsistent description.

Now I'm planning the gray-box script itself: building GameObjects from primitive meshes like cubes, cylinders, and spheres, stripping colliders, and persisting a shared gray material as a prefab sub-asset. For shapes like cones that aren't built-in, I'll generate a simple procedural cone mesh and store it as a sub-asset too.

I'm sketching out the prefab hierarchy — a root object with a Shell group containing the collision-mesh renderers (platform, train, cab, chimney, buffer stop, portal rock), paired with a TrainMassing group for the gray detail bodies, bogies, boiler, smokebox, dome, buffer block, and portal arch frame, plus a pillar base beneath the kill plane.

I'm also planning the broader world layout: a cloud sea plane, distant spires, a viaduct with arches and tunnel cliffs, a hero peak, a ring of ranges, a hamlet ridge with chalets, lighting, and an atmosphere component, then defining the exact world-space bounding box for the corridor and the safety margin background elements must clear.

I'm placing several spires at varying distances and heights to create depth layers—some poking above the cloud plane, others shorter—each topped with a few pines, and roughing out a curved viaduct to the northwest with its deck sitting just below stage level, arches descending into the clouds, and tunnel portals at either end as a mid-ground landmark.

Then I'm positioning a hero peak straight north behind the train for strong central composition, a chalet hamlet glowing on a ridge to the northeast, and distant mountain ranges forming a broken ring at varying heights, with a lower southern range. I'm setting the sun low in the west to drive the sunset lighting direction across the whole scene.

Actually, maybe raise the sun slightly to around 15° from the WSW with a warm orange tone plus blue ambient fill, since a near-horizontal light would leave the platform floor too dim. With the lighting settled, I'll move on to writing the gray-box script itself, keeping it compact.

content.thinking:
The montage labels failed to render due to missing fonts, showing as boxes instead—that's fine for now. Looking at the gray-box render, the cloud sea plane dominates everything below it in white, and the pinnacle flares look too boxy and stepped, like the stage sits on an artificial pedestal rather than emerging as an organic rock spire.

The bigger issue is the flare's top surface at the kill plane reads like a flat "platter" surrounding the stage from elevated angles — exactly the kind of flat, landable ledge I want to avoid since it undermines the sense of danger. I'm considering having the rock walls slope gently outward below the kill plane instead of flaring sharply, so they taper gradually into the clouds rather than forming a visible shelf; alternatively, keeping the walls sheer and vertical all the way down could read better as a dramatic cliff with no ledge at all.

For the cloud sea itself, a flat white plane risks reading as solid, landable ground rather than atmospheric haze, so I need it to look genuinely cloud-like — soft, lumpy, gapped, with pinkish gradient tops and maybe subtle drift. Without volumetrics in URP, I'm thinking layered noise-textured planes at different heights, soft billboard cloud particles near the pinnacle, or stylized low-poly blobby cloud meshes that would fit the game's existing low-poly aesthetic better than a flat textured plane.

I briefly consider making the "below" a modeled valley with a frozen lake, forests, and distant village lights for more depth and life, but that's a much bigger scope than a simple cloud sea, so I'll stick with the dusk cloud sea concept — it's iconic, simpler to build, and reads clearly as a fatal fall zone once the lumpy pink-lit clouds separate it visually from solid ground.

For the kill plane timing, I want fighters to appear to sink into the clouds right as they're KO'd rather than vanishing above them, so I'm placing the cloud tops around −9 to −13, just at or slightly below the kill plane at −10, similar to how Splash Deck handles water sinking before KO.

Next, for the train massing, I'm noting that the train body is currently a simple flat box placeholder, with carriage window band details to be added on the gap side.

Portal Rock is currently just a hexagonal prism standing in for a craggy tunnel entrance with a facade, and the background spires and viaduct are rough stand-ins too regular for production but fine for gray-box depth cues. I'm now reviewing the low-angle views to check how the pinnacle walls read from that perspective.

The low views reveal the flare boxes creating an oversized plinth look that needs fixing, and the spawn/wide views show the cloud plane visually merging with the white platform, which production materials will resolve. Before showing the user, I want to clean up the obvious issues: strip out the flare boxes and extend the pillar walls continuously downward into the cloud layer so they stay flush with the shell footprints.

I also want to lower the cloud sea's top boundary and darken its tone to a bluish mid-gray so it reads distinctly from the lighter platform gray. Looking again at the default spawn view, I'm reconsidering the overall composition — train on the left, platform spanning the center, open void to the right, with the Hero Horn peeking out behind the train.

Thinking about spawn orientation, I wonder if facings should angle more toward the train for a stronger first impression, but since players rotate the camera freely and spawn facing is really just a gameplay convention (facing the opponent), I'll keep the inward-facing setup as is. Now I want to shift focus to whether the shell's actual gameplay holds up, starting with the platform's dimensions.

I'm checking the platform geometry and object placements: the loco's cab and chimney, Portal Rock perched at the NE corner, and the long north-south train roof strip. I'm verifying that the loco overhangs the platform's west end by a reasonable margin, and tracing how the platform's east end meets Portal Rock's footprint to make sure nothing clips or feels cramped at that corner.

Overall the shell feels right, and I want "Mind the Gap" to read clearly in gameplay — a dark void slot between a safety-striped platform edge and the train's flank, with bogies disappearing into shadow below. Before moving to production, I should prepare a handful of gray-box reference views (default, spawn, maybe top-down and low angle) along with a numbered list of composition decisions so the user can lock in the design.

I'll also note the tradeoffs I made, palette and lighting notes, and camera vantage options, then ask for sign-off — possibly offering the user a chance to playtest the gray-box in Training mode first, since the stage is already playable. content.thinking:
Looking at the gray-box massing, I notice the south pillar face is a big blank wall that would need rock cliff texture and station house details in production, while the platform pillar and train pillar read fine as light versus gray blocks.

The viaduct, Horn, spires, and hamlet form the background massing decently, though the mountain cones are too regular for production. I'm fairly comfortable with this massing overall, and the wide shot showing platform, train, Portal Rock, Horn, and viaduct together works as the hero composition.

Now I'm weighing whether to pause and let the user playtest the gray-box shell for early feedback on gap width and roof height, or push straight into production with the understanding that this lock is provisional — since they said "let's push it," momentum matters, but a quiet period with no response would stall things if I stop now.

But production actually requires a locked Stage Design Brief as a hard gate, so I can't skip the sign-off step. I'll draft the brief with status "draft," list the numbered decisions, and message the user with the shell summary, composition choices, and two reference images, asking whether to lock as-is, adjust, or playtest first — treating the in-game visual review as something they can either do now or explicitly defer.

Since the terminal renders GitHub-flavored markdown, I can embed images directly using absolute file paths. I'm thinking about assembling a composite showing the wide view, top-down view, and spawn view, and considering whether to annotate the top-down diagram with labels — which means I'll need to check if suitable fonts are installed before trying to use them for text overlays.

# Last Stop: Mind the Gap

On 2026-10-16 the maintainer asked for a remake of the previous station first pass,
which "was a nice idea but kinda fell flat". The maintainer chose the Mind the Gap
premise, a snowy mountain dusk setting and a lively presentation with weather and
a moving background train. They authorized replacing every asset and the gameplay
geometry. Vendor prefabs are not required. The previous vendor-based presentation and
its rectangular shell are retired.

Yaw follows the stage-design capture convention: yaw 0° puts the camera north of the
stage, looking south. Yaw 180° puts the camera south of the platform, looking north
across it at the train. This is the hero view.

## Personality

The last train has stopped at a summit halt above the clouds, and the gap between
the platform and the train is real.

## Fight premise

One broad island platform is the main floor. It faces the parked last train across
an open 3-unit gap that drops straight into the clouds. A running jump from the
platform edge reaches the carriage roofs, the high road along the north side. The
loco cab is one step higher. Portal Rock, where the train enters its tunnel, is the
high perch. It is reachable from the roof, never from the platform floor. Knockback
toward the train risks the gap: mind the gap. Competitive intent is mixed.

## Composition decisions

1. **Platform:** from yaw 180° the platform fills the foreground and lower third.
   Clean stone slabs carry a white coping edge, a yellow safety line and MIND THE
   GAP lettering along the gap. Snow appears only as flush drifts on the outer edges.
   No furniture stands on the floor.
2. **The gap:** an unmistakable dark cleft separates the platform coping from the
   train's flank and stays open all the way down. The train's lower body, bogies
   and wheels descend into it, then raw rock continues into cloud.
3. **The last train:** a chunky saddle-tank steam locomotive occupies the left third
   from yaw 180°. It has a tall chimney, cab and brass details and pulls two carriages
   in a red-and-cream mountain livery with warm-lit windows. Flat roofs carry snow
   caps; they are the high road. The last carriage disappears into the tunnel portal
   at the right.
4. **End of the line:** the loco noses into a red-and-white buffer stop with a red
   end-of-line lamp at the western tip of the rock, above the drop.
5. **Portal Rock:** a craggy granite buttress closes the right (east) end. A masonry
   tunnel portal opens on its west face. A station-house facade is carved into its
   south face, with warm windows, a door lamp, a station clock and the LAST STOP
   nameboard. Its snowy flat top is the perch.
6. **Scene world below:** the whole summit is one split rock pinnacle. Its sheer walls
   plunge into a sea of clouds just below the KO line. There is no ledge, landing or
   cloud surface above the KO plane.
7. **Scene world around and far:** near rock needles rise from the cloud sea at varied
   distances. From yaw 180°, a curved stone viaduct between two cliffs fills the left
   background, and a small train crosses it periodically. One hero peak, the Horn,
   stands in the center background with alpenglow on its face. The right background
   is a snowy shoulder with a hamlet of chalets, lit windows and chimney smoke. A
   quieter ring of ranges with open gaps surrounds the scene.
8. **Scene world above:** the dusk sky runs from a warm sunset glow in the west to
   deep blue-violet overhead and the first stars with a pale moon in the east. Gentle
   snow falls.
9. **Ambient life (presentation only):** chimney steam and occasional whistle plumes;
   snowfall; the distant train on the viaduct; hamlet chimney smoke and windows;
   a flickering end-of-line lamp; a working station clock; slowly drifting clouds.
10. **Other yaws:** yaw 0° looks across the train's outer side to the platform, the
    sunset ranges and the southern needle. Yaw 90° looks past Portal Rock along the
    train toward the buffer stop and sunset. Yaw 270° looks past the loco nose along
    the train toward the tunnel and the alpenglow peaks.

**Busy here / empty here:** the train, Portal Rock's facade and the distant ring carry
the detail. The platform floor, the gap, the roofs, the immediate recovery corridor
and the cloud surface near the pinnacle stay quiet.

## Negative decisions

- No furniture, lamp posts, benches or standing signs on the platform or train roofs.
  Platform markings are flush.
- No bridge, plank or hidden floor across the gap. No cosmetic surface above the KO
  plane in the gap or around the pillars.
- No background geometry inside the blast corridor. Near the stage, clouds stay
  below the KO plane.
- The parked train never moves. Ambient motion is presentation-only and stays away
  from the fighters.
- One hero landmark, the Horn. The viaduct train is the moving accent, not a
  second hero.
- No vendor or licensed prefabs. Meshes, materials and textures are original and
  stage-owned.
- Snowfall and steam stay sparse near the fight and must never hide a fighter.

## Palette & lighting

Dusk just after sunset. A low warm amber-pink key comes from the western glow, with
blue-violet sky light and cool blue snow shadows. Accents: carriage red, brass, warm
window amber, the red end-of-line lamp and alpenglow pink on the Horn. The platform
stone stays lighter and warmer than the surroundings so fighters and edges read
first.

## Camera vantages

- Yaw 180° hero view across the platform and gap to the train, Horn behind.
- The four spawn views.
- Elevated orbit every 15°; low recovery views every 45°.
- Looking down into the gap from the platform edge and from the roof.
- Top view: footprint, gap, spawns and blast corridor.

## Gameplay shell

| Element | Footprint (X, Z) | Top Y |
|---|---|---|
| Platform | X −16..16, Z −12..0, 2.5 chamfers on the outer corners | 0 |
| Gap | Z 0..3, open to the blast plane | — |
| Train body | X −18..16.5, Z 3..7 | 1.8 |
| Loco cab | X −11..−8 | 2.7 |
| Chimney | X −17.2..−16.2, Z 4.5..5.5 | 2.8 |
| Buffer stop ledge | X −18.8..−18 | 0.4 |
| Portal Rock | six-sided buttress, X 16..22.5, Z 2..10.3 | 3.7 |

The solid volumes reach the KO plane at Y −10. Spawns sit at X ±7, Z −3.5 and −8.5,
facing a point just south of the gap. The baked arena owns the derived boundaries.

## Movement basis

Deterministic Shared checks on the baked shell, for the current FightGuy, Manki,
Wibou and Bonk definitions, establish the following:
- A running jump from the platform edge lands on the carriage roof for every character.
- One jump from the roof reaches the cab and Portal Rock. FightGuy has the smallest margin.
- No standing or air jump reaches Portal Rock from the platform floor. Only Bonk's
  double jump has the height.
- The gap is lethal with no hidden floor.
- One air jump from just below the lip recovers onto the platform.
- The outer walls stop inward recovery and allow a retreat.

These are structural checks, not human PVP acceptance.

content.thinking:
I'm marking the design brief as locked and approved, then moving into the production plan—starting with art direction details like the low-poly style, material setup, and unit scale conventions.

Next I'm planning the Blender modelling pipeline for the platform assets, listing out the FBX files needed: the platform geometry with slab textures, edge coping, the yellow safety line and signage decals, and the rock pillar walls that need to align with the collision volume. I'm working through how the visual rock relief should sit slightly inward from the collision boundary rather than protruding outward, so players never visually clip into the walls while sliding against them.

For the train asset, I'm detailing the full locomotive model (boiler, cab, wheels, buffers) plus two carriages with windows, roofs, bogies, and gangway bellows, along with the track bed, rails, ballast, and the supporting rock pillar beneath it. I'm mapping out exact coordinate ranges so the visual geometry stays flush with the collision strip's edges while the rock walls recede inward below the track bed.

I'm noting a mismatch: the roof collision is continuous across the gangway gap, but a narrower gangway cover plate would leave a small gap where the player could stand on nothing, so I'll widen the gangway roof cover to match the full collision width instead.

Turning to the loco, I'm mapping out collision heights for the tank, cab, and chimney, then sketching the visual profile—a rounded saddle tank over the boiler, a smokebox front near the chimney, and the running board positioned along the loco's underside.

Below the footplate I'm placing the driving wheels, frames, and cylinders, while above it goes the saddle tank, the cylindrical smokebox with its flared chimney and smokebox door, and a brass steam dome on top of the tank.

I'm checking that the steam dome stays flush with or barely above the collision top so it doesn't create a visible bump, considering a brass band ring instead. Then I'm laying out the cab with its spectacle windows and roof kept flush, the coal bunker with its heap capped at the collision height, and the front buffers.

For the headlamp on the smokebox front, I'm noting it slightly protrudes above the buffer shelf's collision top, which could let a player clip it, but I'm treating this as a minor acceptable issue or mounting it flush instead. Then I'm designing the buffer stop block at the end of the shelf with red-white stripes and a lamp on top, checking that its protrusion height is also reasonable.

For the LastStopPortalRock asset, I'm shaping a craggy rock buttress matching the collision prism, with flat snow on top, a stone arch tunnel portal flush with the rock's west face, and a dark recessed tunnel interior where the train visually disappears as it enters, even though its collision continues inside.

On the station facade's south face I'm placing windows with emissive panes, a door, lamp, clock, and the LAST STOP board, keeping everything flush or inset within 0.15 of the surface. I'm also checking that the collision wall above the rock's tunnel opening blocks players from walking into the tunnel, since the train itself fills the lower portion of the archway.

The arch above the carriage roof leaves a small dark visual gap that doesn't match the collision, but since it's dark and too shallow to read as passable, I'll tighten the arch height to about 2.1 so the gap stays minimal and stylistically acceptable. Now I'm checking the deep rock pillars extending from -10 to -40 to make sure they stay flush with the collision volume.

I'm organizing the pillar meshes per structure—platform, train, and portal rock—each extending down to -40 with craggy relief and snow ledges carved inward. I'm also noting that icicles hanging below the platform's north edge could let a falling fighter visually clip through them, which is a minor acceptable visual quirk.

Then I'm planning the remaining assets: a sky dome with gradient and moon/star UVs, a cloud sea built from lumpy low-poly puffs over a base plane, the mountain range with rock and snow materials split by slope, and the curved viaduct with its arches and tunnel portal cliffs.

Given how much modeling this is, I'm splitting it into two passes: Pass A covers the core shell (platform, pillars, train, rock facade, buffer stop), sky, clouds, mountains, lighting, and particle effects, while Pass B adds the viaduct, distant train mover script, hamlet, pines, and clock details.

For the Blender workflow, I'm planning Python scripts that build each asset in a fresh scene and export to FBX, run headlessly via command line with bpy/bmesh. I need to handle the Z-up to Y-up coordinate conversion for Unity compatibility, using the standard FBX export settings with forward and up axes configured correctly plus baked space transforms.

Since the axis conversion is error-prone to reason out theoretically, the safer approach is to test with a known asymmetric marker object placed at a specific Blender coordinate and check where it lands in Unity, then build a helper function to convert Unity stage coordinates into Blender coordinates based on that observed mapping. I also consider alternatives like OBJ or glTF export, but FBX remains the standard choice despite its axis quirks.

For export settings, I'll use scale factor 1 with "Apply Scalings: FBX All" and "Apply Transform" checked, forward −Z and up Y, which should give Unity an imported object with identity rotation and scale 1 — something I'll confirm with the test. For materials, I'm noting that Blender material names should carry over so Unity's importer can recognize and map them appropriately.

Simpler approach: import with no materials, then assign stage-owned materials to each renderer manually by matching FBX material slot names to submesh order in the prefab assembly.

For textures, I'm weighing options between Blender's Python/numpy pipeline, ImageMagick's procedural noise generators, or doing it directly in C# — leaning toward Blender Python with numpy for finer control over the noise generation.

For the mountain faces, I'll assign materials per face based on normal direction (snow vs rock), which Unity will treat as two submeshes. Then in the Unity assembly step, a C# editor script builds the prefab by instantiating the imported FBX model prefabs as children, preserving their asset links.

For dynamic elements, I'm setting up particle systems through script configuration using URP's unlit particle shader with a generated soft circle texture, plus ambient runtime scripts like a path-follower component that moves objects along waypoints with configurable speed and pause, supporting trailing "carriage" children offset along the same path for things like a distant train.

I'm also adding a clock script that ticks hour/minute hands with real system time, a flicker script that pulses light and emissive intensity using Perlin noise, and no-script particle effects like steam puffs with burst emission, whistle plumes on timed intervals, and falling snow using a box emitter with noise-driven turbulence in world space.

These scripts should go in the World runtime folder under the client's namespace, kept small and purely presentational. I also want to check how the Log Off presentation stage sets up its shaders and materials so the station matches the existing stylized URP look.

Brief is locked, so I'm moving into production. First I'll run an FBX axis/scale round-trip test from headless Blender into Unity to ensure models import directly into stage coordinates without needing per-object fixes.

I'm thinking through the pillar walls now — carving rock from the coping line down to −40 following the platform's six-sided polygon, with the gap-facing wall getting a masonry upper band over cut rock, and the train side similarly layered with trackbed detail. # Original procedural textures for Last Stop (Blender headless; numpy only, no external images).
import bpy, sys, os, math
import numpy as np

OUT = sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--') + 1]
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
RNG = np.random.default_rng(16102026)


def vnoise(h, w, cy, cx, rng):
    """Tileable value noise: cy x cx lattice cells over an h x w image (smoothstep interpolation)."""
    lat = rng.random((cy, cx)).astype(np.float32)
    ty = np.arange(h, dtype=np.float32) * cy / h
    tx = np.arange(w, dtype=np.float32) * cx / w
    y0 = np.floor(ty).astype(np.int64); fy = ty - y0; fy = fy * fy * (3 - 2 * fy)
    x0 = np.floor(tx).astype(np.int64); fx = tx - x0; fx = fx * fx * (3 - 2 * fx)
    y0 %= cy; x0 %= cx; y1 = (y0 + 1) % cy; x1 = (x0 + 1) % cx
    v00 = lat[y0[:, None], x0[None, :]]; v01 = lat[y0[:, None], x1[None, :]]
    v10 = lat[y1[:, None], x0[None, :]]; v11 = lat[y1[:, None], x1[None, :]]
    fx = fx[None, :]; fy = fy[:, None]
    return (v00 * (1 - fx) + v01 * fx) * (1 - fy) + (v10 * (1 - fx) + v11 * fx) * fy


def fbm(h, w, cy, cx, octaves, rng, gain=0.5):
    total = np.zeros((h, w), np.float32); amp = 1.0; norm = 0.0
    for o in range(octaves):
        total += amp * vnoise(h, w, cy * 2 ** o, cx * 2 ** o, rng); norm += amp; amp *= gain
    return total / norm


def hexc(s):
    s = s.lstrip('#')
    return np.array([int(s[i:i + 2], 16) / 255.0 for i in (0, 2, 4)], np.float32)


def lerp(a, b, t):
    t = np.clip(t, 0, 1)[..., None] if np.ndim(t) else t
    return a * (1 - t) + b * t


def save(name, rgb, alpha=None):
    h, w = rgb.shape[:2]
    rgba = np.ones((h, w, 4), np.float32)
    rgba[..., :3] = np.clip(rgb, 0, 1)
    if alpha is not None:
        rgba[..., 3] = np.clip(alpha, 0, 1)
    img = bpy.data.images.new(name, width=w, height=h, alpha=alpha is not None, float_buffer=False)
    img.pixels.foreach_set(np.flipud(rgba).ravel())
    path = os.path.join(OUT, name + '.png')
    img.filepath_raw = path
    img.file_format = 'PNG'
    img.save()
    print('wrote', path, w, h)


# 1) Platform slabs: 6 x 6 world units per tile, running-bond slabs 1.5 x 1.0.
def platform_slabs(size=1024, units=6.0):
    px = size / units
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:size, 0:size].astype(np.float32)
    row = np.floor(yy / px).astype(int)  # 1.0-unit rows
    offset = (row % 2) * 0.75 * px
    col = np.floor(((xx + offset) % size) / (1.5 * px)).astype(int)
    slab_id = row * 31 + col * 7
    tint = (np.sin(slab_id * 12.9898) * 43758.5453) % 1.0
    base = lerp(hexc('#c8c1b2'), hexc('#d6cfc0'), tint)
    n = fbm(size, size, 8, 8, 5, RNG)
    speck = fbm(size, size, 64, 64, 2, RNG)
    base = base * (0.93 + 0.12 * n[..., None]) - (speck[..., None] > 0.72) * 0.05
    # grout distance (rows every px, slab ends every 1.5 px with row offset)
    gy = np.abs(((yy + px * 0.5) % px) - px * 0.5)
    gx = np.abs((((xx + offset) % (1.5 * px)) + 0.75 * px) % (1.5 * px) - 0.75 * px)
    gdist = np.minimum(gy, gx)
    grout = np.clip(1.0 - (gdist - 1.5) / 3.0, 0, 1)
    frost = fbm(size, size, 16, 16, 3, RNG)
    grout_col = lerp(hexc('#8b857b'), hexc('#dfe6ee'), (frost > 0.55) * 0.8)
    rgb = lerp(base, grout_col, grout)
    # soft bevel highlight just inside each slab edge
    bevel = np.clip(1.0 - (gdist - 3.0) / 5.0, 0, 1) * (1 - grout)
    rgb = rgb + bevel[..., None] * 0.035
    save('LastStopPlatformSlabs', rgb)


# 2) Granite: blue-grey rock with horizontal strata; tiles 8 world units.
def granite(size=1024):
    n1 = fbm(size, size, 4, 4, 6, RNG)
    n2 = fbm(size, size, 16, 16, 4, RNG)
    strata_warp = fbm(size, size, 2, 6, 3, RNG)
    yy = np.mgrid[0:size, 0:size][0].astype(np.float32) / size
    strata = 0.5 + 0.5 * np.sin((yy * 9 + strata_warp * 1.6) * math.tau)
    t = 0.55 * n1 + 0.25 * strata + 0.2 * n2
    rgb = lerp(hexc('#3a4150'), hexc('#6d7686'), (t - 0.25) / 0.55)
    flecks = vnoise(size, size, 256, 256, RNG)
    rgb = rgb + (flecks > 0.9)[..., None] * 0.06 - (flecks < 0.06)[..., None] * 0.04
    cracks = np.abs(fbm(size, size, 6, 6, 4, RNG) - 0.5)
    rgb = rgb * (0.75 + 0.25 * np.clip(cracks * 14, 0, 1))[..., None]
    save('LastStopGranite', rgb)


# 3) Snow: cool white with soft blue shading and sparse sparkles.
def snow(size=512):
    n = fbm(size, size, 4, 4, 5, RNG)
    rgb = lerp(hexc('#c9d5e8'), hexc('#f2f6fb'), (n - 0.3) / 0.45)
    sp = vnoise(size, size, 192, 192, RNG)
    rgb = rgb + (sp > 0.93)[..., None] * 0.08
    save('LastStopSnow', rgb)


# 4) Ashlar masonry: 4 x 4 world units; courses 0.5, blocks 0.9 long.
def masonry(size=512, units=4.0):
    px = size / units
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:size, 0:size].astype(np.float32)
    ch = 0.5 * px; bw = 0.9 * px
    row = np.floor(yy / ch).astype(int)
    off = (row % 2) * bw * 0.5
    col = np.floor(((xx + off) % size) / bw).astype(int)
    bid = row * 17 + col * 5
    tint = (np.sin(bid * 7.31) * 9187.13) % 1.0
    base = lerp(hexc('#6c6a66'), hexc('#8e8a83'), tint)
    n = fbm(size, size, 8, 8, 4, RNG)
    base = base * (0.9 + 0.18 * n[..., None])
    gy = np.abs(((yy + ch * 0.5) % ch) - ch * 0.5)
    gx = np.abs((((xx + off) % bw) + bw * 0.5) % bw - bw * 0.5)
    g = np.clip(1.0 - (np.minimum(gy, gx) - 1.0) / 2.5, 0, 1)
    rgb = lerp(base, hexc('#3b3a39'), g)
    save('LastStopMasonry', rgb)


# 5) Dusk sky panorama: u = azimuth (north at 0.5, east 0.75, west 0.25), v = elevation (-15..90 deg).
def sky(w=2048, h=1024):
    v = (np.arange(h, dtype=np.float32)[::-1] + 0.5) / h  # row 0 = top (v=1)
    u = (np.arange(w, dtype=np.float32) + 0.5) / w
    elev = -15 + v * 105.0  # degrees
    az = (u - 0.5) * 360.0  # 0 = north, +90 east, -90 west
    E = elev[:, None]; A = az[None, :]
    west = np.exp(-((((A + 90 + 180) % 360) - 180) / 70.0) ** 2)  # glow lobe around west
    hgt = np.clip(E / 90.0, 0, 1)
    # base vertical gradient (east/neutral)
    zen = hexc('#121a3c'); mid = hexc('#2c3a6e'); hor = hexc('#5b5f92')
    t1 = np.clip(hgt / 0.35, 0, 1); t2 = np.clip((hgt - 0.35) / 0.65, 0, 1)
    base = lerp(lerp(hor, mid, t1), zen, t2)
    # sunset glow: warm near the horizon in the west, lavender above
    glow_h = np.exp(-np.clip(E, 0, None) / 9.0)
    glow_m = np.exp(-np.clip(E, 0, None) / 28.0)
    warm = lerp(hexc('#f0a35e'), hexc('#ff7f6b'), np.clip((E + 2) / 10.0, 0, 1))
    lav = hexc('#9a7fb3')
    rgb = base
    rgb = lerp(rgb, lav, glow_m * west * 0.75)
    rgb = lerp(rgb, warm, glow_h * west * 0.95)
    # faint pink belt (anti-twilight arch) in the east just above the horizon
    east = np.exp(-((((A - 90 + 180) % 360) - 180) / 80.0) ** 2)
    belt = np.exp(-((E - 6.0) / 6.0) ** 2) * east
    rgb = lerp(rgb, hexc('#b48aa7'), belt * 0.35)
    # below horizon: darker haze (mostly hidden by clouds)
    below = np.clip(-E / 15.0, 0, 1)
    rgb = lerp(rgb, hexc('#2a2f52'), below * 0.7)
    # wispy high cloud streaks lit pink in the west
    streak = fbm(h, w, 6, 24, 4, RNG)
    streak = np.clip((streak - 0.58) * 4, 0, 1) * np.exp(-((E - 18) / 12.0) ** 2)
    rgb = lerp(rgb, lerp(hexc('#6a5f8f'), hexc('#ffb38a'), west), streak * 0.45)
    # stars: denser overhead and east, fading toward the western glow and horizon
    st = RNG.random((h, w)).astype(np.float32)
    star_mask = (st > 0.9985) * np.clip((E - 12) / 30.0, 0, 1) * (1 - west * 0.95)
    tw = RNG.random((h, w)).astype(np.float32)
    rgb = rgb + star_mask[..., None] * (0.55 + 0.45 * tw[..., None])
    save('LastStopSky', rgb)


# 6) Cloud tops: soft billows (tileable), used for the cloud sea and puffs.
def clouds(size=1024):
    n = fbm(size, size, 4, 4, 6, RNG)
    b = fbm(size, size, 12, 12, 3, RNG)
    t = np.clip((0.7 * n + 0.3 * b - 0.32) / 0.45, 0, 1)
    rgb = lerp(hexc('#8d92b8'), hexc('#f3e6ea'), t)
    alpha = np.clip((0.75 * n + 0.25 * b - 0.3) / 0.25, 0, 1)
    save('LastStopCloudTops', rgb, alpha)


# 7) Soft particle sprite.
def soft_dot(size=128):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:size, 0:size].astype(np.float32)
    r = np.sqrt((xx - size / 2 + 0.5) ** 2 + (yy - size / 2 + 0.5) ** 2) / (size / 2)
    a = np.clip(1 - r, 0, 1) ** 1.6
    save('LastStopSoftDot', np.ones((size, size, 3), np.float32), a)


# 8) Swiss-style station clock face (hands are separate meshes).
def clock_face(size=512):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:size, 0:size].astype(np.float32)
    cx = cy = size / 2 - 0.5
    dx = xx - cx; dy = cy - yy
    r = np.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy) / (size / 2)
    ang = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(dx, dy)) + 360) % 360  # 0 at 12 o'clock, clockwise
    rgb = np.ones((size, size, 3), np.float32) * hexc('#f6f4ee')
    ink = np.zeros((size, size), np.float32)
    # minute ticks
    m = (ang % 6.0); md = np.minimum(m, 6.0 - m)
    arc = md * math.pi / 180 * r * size / 2  # distance in px from tick centreline
    ink = np.maximum(ink, ((arc < 2.2) & (r > 0.84) & (r < 0.93)).astype(np.float32))
    # hour bars
    hm = (ang % 30.0); hd = np.minimum(hm, 30.0 - hm)
    harc = hd * math.pi / 180 * r * size / 2
    ink = np.maximum(ink, ((harc < 7.5) & (r > 0.66) & (r < 0.93)).astype(np.float32))
    rim = ((r > 0.955) & (r < 1.0)).astype(np.float32)
    rgb = lerp(rgb, hexc('#1b1b1d'), np.maximum(ink, rim))
    alpha = (r < 1.0).astype(np.float32)
    save('LastStopClockFace', rgb, alpha)


platform_slabs(); granite(); snow(); masonry(); sky(); clouds(); soft_dot(); clock_face()

import numpy as np

OUT = sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--') + 1]

RNG = np.random.default_rng(16102026)


def vnoise(h, w, cy, cx, rng):
    """Tileable value noise: cy x cx lattice cells over an h x w image (smoothstep interpolation)."""
    lat = rng.random((cy, cx)).astype(np.float32)
    ty = np.arange(h, dtype=np.float32) * cy / h
    tx = np.arange(w, dtype=np.float32) * cx / w
    y0 = np.floor(ty).astype(np.int64); fy = ty - y0; fy = fy * fy * (3 - 2 * fy)
    x0 = np.floor(tx).astype(np.int64); fx = tx - x0; fx = fx * fx * (3 - 2 * fx)
    y0 %= cy; x0 %= cx; y1 = (y0 + 1) % cy; x1 = (x0 + 1) % cx
    v00 = lat[y0[:, None], x0[None, :]]; v01 = lat[y0[:, None], x1[None, :]]
    v10 = lat[y1[:, None], x0[None, :]]; v11 = lat[y1[:, None], x1[None, :]]
    fx = fx[None, :]; fy = fy[:, None]
    return (v00 * (1 - fx) + v01 * fx) * (1 - fy) + (v10 * (1 - fx) + v11 * fx) * fy

    if alpha is not None:

    img = bpy.data.images.new(name, width=w, height=h, alpha=alpha is not None, float_buffer=False)

For UVs, I'm using box projection based on dominant normal axis — top faces use x/z, side faces use the horizontal axis paired with y, both scaled consistently with Unity's coordinate convention.

For shading, I'm planning flat shading by default but smooth shading for curved parts like the boiler and wheels, using per-face smoothing flags since Blender 4.1+ dropped auto-smooth, exporting with face-based smoothing so Unity's FBX importer picks up the correct normals.

I'm also considering bevels via bmesh operations on selected edges to add highlights to chunky shapes like the train body and cab, keeping bevels inward so they don't affect collision silhouettes, and planning to generate 3D text using a loaded font, extruded and converted to mesh.

For converting the text to mesh, I realize using the evaluated depsgraph approach (`evaluated_get` plus `new_from_object`) avoids operator context issues in background mode, then I'll transform the resulting mesh into position. For exports, I'm planning one FBX per asset group with multiple child objects, joining meshes by material to keep renderer counts low in the resulting Unity prefab.

Now I'm sketching out the first asset, LastStopPlatform.fbx, working through the walkable top surface and the coping band around its edges — since overlapping coplanar faces would cause z-fighting, I need to inset the main platform polygon and build the coping as separate strip meshes around the perimeter instead.

I'm defining a polygon offset function to shrink the hexagonal footprint inward for the top surface, with the north edge (facing the gap) getting a wider 0.55 coping band versus 0.45 elsewhere, then building the coping geometry as a top band between outer and inset edges plus a beveled outer vertical face dropping down to y=−0.35.

Now I'm planning the safety line as a yellow painted decal strip along the gap edge, and figuring out where to place the "MIND THE GAP" text on the coping band, positioning it just inside the yellow line so it reads naturally on the platform edge like the London Underground signage.

For the text orientation, I need to work out the axis mapping between Blender's text plane and Unity's coordinate system so the letters face upright and read correctly from a viewer standing south looking north, with three repeated instances spaced along the platform.

But I'm now worried about a reflection issue — flipping axes between the two coordinate systems could mirror the text instead of properly rotating it, so I need to carefully check the handedness of the transform.

Working through the coordinate conversion carefully, a glyph point at local (gx, gy) in Blender after the 180° rotation and translation maps to Unity coordinates (x0 + gx, z0 + gy) on the floor plane, meaning reading runs along +X and up runs along +Z — so the mapping preserves orientation correctly rather than mirroring, which is what I needed to confirm.

For the snow drifts, I'm placing flush white irregular patches near the outer edges and south chamfers at a slight height, opting for opaque stylized polygons over alpha-blended decals to avoid sorting issues. Then I'm moving to the pillar structure, defining the rock walls beneath the coping down to y=−40, with masonry texturing on the north gap-facing wall for the top portion.

Past the kill plane around y=−10, I'm flaring the rock outward progressively toward −40 to form a spire base, relying on the cloud layer to hide the lower detail.

I briefly consider adding warm inset windows on the platform's south face like a cliff dwelling, but since the design brief puts the station facade on Portal Rock rather than the pillar, I decide to keep the south face plain rock with small icicles at the coping lip instead.

Now I'm working out the train layout along X for LastStopTrain.fbx — placing the buffer stop, then the locomotive's front buffer beam and smokebox positions, matching up the buffers so they touch the stop.

I notice a mismatch: the smokebox's cylindrical radius is narrower than the collision box width, so at the roof edges the player would float above the curved surface instead of standing on it. I need to widen the saddle tank shape to cover that gap.

I'll make the saddle tank body span the full loco length with rounded top edges, placing a round smokebox door with a handle on the front face, and position the chimney near the front on top.

Painting a black smokebox band at the front, adding thin brass rings around the tank body (kept within collision tolerance), and shaping the chimney as a flared cylinder near the top.

I'm placing a flattened brass steam dome disc into the tank top and skipping the safety valve, then roughing out the cab as a boxy section with roof and checking the front spectacle windows stay within the cab's face bounds.

Now I'm detailing cab windows, with round front ones showing an inner firebox glow and side openings revealing the dark cab interior lit by orange emissive panels; the cab itself is red with a black roof. I'm adding the coal bunker and lumpy black coal pile, the footplate running board beneath, and starting to lay out the frames and driving wheel positions underneath.

I'm now placing three driving wheels per side with red spoked wheels, coupling rods, cylinders up front, and front buffers protruding from the loco's nose.

The buffer beam sits at the front of the loco body, and since the buffers fall below the shelf's top edge, they end up tucked inside the buffer stop collision region, which works out visually. I still need to handle the gangway gap between the loco and the first carriage, making sure the roof plate stays continuous across it.

Now I'm laying out carriage 1: about 9.9 units long with a rounded roof, painted in the classic red-cream-red color bands with a gray roof and snow cap on top, plus five evenly spaced windows per side glowing with warm emissive glass.

Adding end doors with small windows, a "LAST STOP" destination board in cream text on dark red above the window band, black underframe, and two bogies with double-axle wheel sets beneath the carriage.

Now I'm adding snow coverage on the roof top surface, positioning the second gangway and carriage (which extends into the tunnel portal with six windows per side), and working out track gauge proportions for the rails.

I'm settling on rail positions aligned with wheel treads, then laying out the sleeper spacing, ballast bed dimensions, and gravel texture for the track.

For the pillar supporting the train section, I'm defining it as solid rock dropping from the track bed down to the ground, with inward relief carved into the south and north faces and the west end merging into the Portal Rock pillar on the east. I'm also working out the buffer stop at the west end — a concrete block rising from the collision shelf up to the track bed, topped with the actual buffer structure.

I'm fixing this by adding a concrete cap beam spanning the full shelf width at the top, acting as the buffer stop's base platform.

I'm now shifting attention to the Portal Rock and facade, treating it as a separate asset, and starting to think through how the second carriage of the train continues from there.

Below the top snow cap I'm adding a cornice band from 3.7 down to 3.4 before transitioning to rock, then placing the tunnel portal on the west face of the hexagon, centered around z=5 with roughly a 4.4 unit wide arch opening.

I'm detailing the masonry arch ring with voussoirs around the opening, a keystone, and a flush stone facade set into the rock, plus considering a small date stone above the arch (maybe "1898") though I'll skip adding actual text there. Then I'm carving out the dark tunnel interior as a box recessed into the rock mass.

For the station itself, I'm mapping the south-facing hexagon edges to place the facade—door and window openings sized relative to figure height—onto the edge closest to facing south, with another edge angled southeast.

I'm reconsidering a door opening onto the void with no floor doesn't make sense, so I'll drop the door and use windows instead, plus a clock and nameboard positioned across the available facade width.

I'm placing two windows, a nameboard above, and a clock on the SE edge, then thinking through whether a door could instead sit on the west face near the train portal, opening onto the roof area above it.

Dropping that idea since there's no good access there. I'll settle on windows, clock, nameboard, and a lantern to give the facade its "station house" feel, maybe adding a small chimney with smoke on the rock's north corner, but skipping flagpole or signal ideas on top. Then I move on to cataloging the remaining assets: the sky dome with moon, the mountain ranges and near needles, and the cloud layers with mist.

Next I'm planning the viaduct and distant train assets, plus the hamlet with chalets and pines. For materials, I'm setting up a Unity URP list matching FBX material names — platform slabs, cream stone coping, safety yellow, and a white paint material, debating whether "MIND THE GAP" text should be yellow-on-dark or the traditional white-on-platform-edge look.

Now I'm continuing the material list: snow, granite, masonry, and the train body colors (glossy red, cream, black), plus brass and steel metallics, roof gray, and a warm emissive window material for bloom, moving toward a fire glow emission material next.

Still defining more materials...

Then I'm rounding out the list with clouds, mist, wood chalets, pine trees, viaduct stone, and clock hands — roughly 35 materials total, which seems reasonable. Now I'm turning to fog setup, thinking a linear atmospheric fog through ArenaAtmosphere.

On the sky dome though, I realize fog could be a problem: URP Unlit shaders still include fog keywords by default, so a dome placed far away would get fully fogged into a solid color and erase the sky entirely. Rather than fighting that with a custom shader, I'll skip global fog altogether and instead bake atmospheric perspective directly into the mountain layer materials, making farther ranges progressively bluer and lighter to fake the depth effect.

Now I'm thinking through the light setup: a warm low directional sun from the west at roughly 12° elevation with soft shadows, plus a secondary fill directional light from the east with no shadows to balance it.

Then I'm adding atmospheric trilight ambient (sky/equator/ground tones) and a handful of point lights for warmth and story — carriage window spill, Portal Rock lantern, the red end-of-line lamp with flicker, and the cab fire glow — while being mindful of URP's per-object point light limits.

I'm also weighing whether the stage should temporarily disable the scene's existing directional lights so the dusk mood isn't washed out in Training/Solo, since Log Off's precedent was to just add its own light atop the scene's rather than override them.

Given AGENTS.md's guidance to reuse existing infrastructure before adding abstractions, I'll hold off on that cross-cutting change and first just check the URP asset's additional-light limits and shadow settings before deciding.

The sky now reads as dusk with a warm western glow, pink streaks, and stars to the east. Before modelling further, I'll check the URP pipeline's limits on additional lights and shadows, since the dusk effect relies on a few warm point lights.

"""Last Stop Blender helpers: build meshes directly in Unity stage coordinates.

Unity (x, y, z) -> Blender (-x, -z, y)  (verified with an FBX round trip: Blender (1,2,3) -> Unity (-1,3,-2)).
All helper inputs are Unity coordinates; faces are oriented by an explicit outward direction.
"""
import bpy, bmesh, math, sys, os
from mathutils import Vector, Matrix, noise

ROOT = '/home/binoui/Projects/SlopArena/client/Unity/Assets/Stages/last_stop'


def B(p):
    return Vector((-p[0], -p[2], p[1]))


def BD(d):
    # Directions transform with the same linear map.
    return Vector((-d[0], -d[2], d[1]))


def reset():
    bpy.ops.wm.read_factory_settings(use_empty=True)


def get_mat(name):
    m = bpy.data.materials.get(name)
    if m is None:
        m = bpy.data.materials.new(name)
    return m


class MB:
    """Mesh builder in Unity coordinates with per-face material slots and world UVs."""

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.bm = bmesh.new()
        self.uv = self.bm.loops.layers.uv.new('UVMap')
        self.mats = []

    def mi(self, mat):
        if mat not in self.mats:
            self.mats.append(mat)
        return self.mats.index(mat)

    def face(self, pts, mat, outward=None, uvs=None, uv_scale=1.0, smooth=False, uv_mode='auto'):
        verts = [self.bm.verts.new(B(p)) for p in pts]
        if outward is not None:
            # Newell normal in Unity space; flip vertex order so it matches `outward`.
            n = Vector((0, 0, 0))
            for i in range(len(pts)):
                a = Vector(pts[i]); b = Vector(pts[(i + 1) % len(pts)])
                n.x += (a.y - b.y) * (a.z + b.z); n.y += (a.z - b.z) * (a.x + b.x); n.z += (a.x - b.x) * (a.y + b.y)
            # Unity is left-handed vs. the Blender frame: compare in Blender space instead.
            fb = bmesh.ops.contextual_create  # placeholder to keep linters calm
        f = self.bm.faces.new(verts)
        f.material_index = self.mi(mat)
        f.smooth = smooth
        f.normal_update()
        if outward is not None:
            if f.normal.dot(BD(outward)) < 0:
                f.normal_flip()
        # UVs
        if uvs is None:
            nrm = Vector(outward) if outward is not None else Vector((0, 1, 0))
            ax = max(range(3), key=lambda k: abs(nrm[k]))
            uvs = []
            for p in pts:
                if uv_mode == 'auto':
                    if ax == 1:
                        uvs.append((p[0] / uv_scale, p[2] / uv_scale))
                    elif ax == 0:
                        uvs.append((p[2] / uv_scale * (1 if nrm[0] > 0 else -1), p[1] / uv_scale))
                    else:
                        uvs.append((p[0] / uv_scale * (-1 if nrm[2] > 0 else 1), p[1] / uv_scale))
        # Re-read loops in final order (normal_flip reverses loops).
        vmap = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(verts)}
        for loop in f.loops:
            loop[self.uv].uv = uvs[vmap[loop.vert]]
        return f

    def quad_strip_uv(self, pts, mat, outward, u0, u1, v0, v1, smooth=False):
        return self.face(pts, mat, outward, uvs=[(u0, v0), (u1, v0), (u1, v1), (u0, v1)], smooth=smooth)

    def box(self, mn, mx, mat, uv_scale=1.0, skip=(), mats=None):
        x0, y0, z0 = mn; x1, y1, z1 = mx
        faces = {
            'top': ([(x0, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z1)], (0, 1, 0)),
            'bottom': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z1), (x0, y0, z1)], (0, -1, 0)),
            'west': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x0, y1, z0), (x0, y1, z1), (x0, y0, z1)], (-1, 0, 0)),
            'east': ([(x1, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z1), (x1, y0, z1)], (1, 0, 0)),
            'south': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x0, y1, z0)], (0, 0, -1)),
            'north': ([(x0, y0, z1), (x1, y0, z1), (x1, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z1)], (0, 0, 1)),
        }
        for k, (pts, n) in faces.items():
            if k in skip:
                continue
            m = mats.get(k, mat) if mats else mat
            self.face(pts, m, n, uv_scale=uv_scale)

    def cylinder(self, c, axis, r, length, mat, seg=16, caps=True, cap_mat=None, smooth=True, r2=None, start_angle=0.0):
        """Cylinder/frustum from c (base centre) along a unit axis ('x','y','z' or vector)."""
        a = {'x': Vector((1, 0, 0)), 'y': Vector((0, 1, 0)), 'z': Vector((0, 0, 1))}.get(axis, None)
        a = Vector(axis).normalized() if a is None else a
        t = Vector((0, 1, 0)) if abs(a.y) < 0.9 else Vector((1, 0, 0))
        u = a.cross(t).normalized(); v = a.cross(u).normalized()
        r2 = r if r2 is None else r2
        c = Vector(c); e = c + a * length
        ring0 = []; ring1 = []
        for i in range(seg):
            ang = start_angle + i / seg * math.tau
            d = u * math.cos(ang) + v * math.sin(ang)
            ring0.append(c + d * r); ring1.append(e + d * r2)
        for i in range(seg):
            j = (i + 1) % seg
            mid = (ring0[i] + ring0[j] + ring1[i] + ring1[j]) / 4
            out = mid - (c + a * (length / 2))
            out = out - a * out.dot(a)
            self.face([tuple(ring0[i]), tuple(ring0[j]), tuple(ring1[j]), tuple(ring1[i])], mat, tuple(out),

"""Last Stop Blender helpers: build meshes directly in Unity stage coordinates.

Unity (x, y, z) -> Blender (-x, -z, y)  (verified with an FBX round trip: Blender (1,2,3) -> Unity (-1,3,-2)).
All helper inputs are Unity coordinates; faces are oriented by an explicit outward direction.
"""
import bpy, bmesh, math, sys, os
from mathutils import Vector, Matrix, noise

ROOT = '/home/binoui/Projects/SlopArena/client/Unity/Assets/Stages/last_stop'


def B(p):
    return Vector((-p[0], -p[2], p[1]))


def BD(d):
    # Directions transform with the same linear map.
    return Vector((-d[0], -d[2], d[1]))


def reset():
    bpy.ops.wm.read_factory_settings(use_empty=True)


def get_mat(name):
    m = bpy.data.materials.get(name)
    if m is None:
        m = bpy.data.materials.new(name)
    return m


class MB:
    """Mesh builder in Unity coordinates with per-face material slots and world UVs."""

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.bm = bmesh.new()
        self.uv = self.bm.loops.layers.uv.new('UVMap')
        self.mats = []

    def mi(self, mat):
        if mat not in self.mats:
            self.mats.append(mat)
        return self.mats.index(mat)

    def face(self, pts, mat, outward=None, uvs=None, uv_scale=1.0, smooth=False, uv_mode='auto'):
        verts = [self.bm.verts.new(B(p)) for p in pts]
        if outward is not None:
            # Newell normal in Unity space; flip vertex order so it matches `outward`.
            n = Vector((0, 0, 0))
            for i in range(len(pts)):
                a = Vector(pts[i]); b = Vector(pts[(i + 1) % len(pts)])
                n.x += (a.y - b.y) * (a.z + b.z); n.y += (a.z - b.z) * (a.x + b.x); n.z += (a.x - b.x) * (a.y + b.y)
            # Unity is left-handed vs. the Blender frame: compare in Blender space instead.
            fb = bmesh.ops.contextual_create  # placeholder to keep linters calm
        f = self.bm.faces.new(verts)
        f.material_index = self.mi(mat)
        f.smooth = smooth
        f.normal_update()
        if outward is not None:
            if f.normal.dot(BD(outward)) < 0:
                f.normal_flip()
        # UVs
        if uvs is None:
            nrm = Vector(outward) if outward is not None else Vector((0, 1, 0))
            ax = max(range(3), key=lambda k: abs(nrm[k]))
            uvs = []
            for p in pts:
                if uv_mode == 'auto':
                    if ax == 1:
                        uvs.append((p[0] / uv_scale, p[2] / uv_scale))
                    elif ax == 0:
                        uvs.append((p[2] / uv_scale * (1 if nrm[0] > 0 else -1), p[1] / uv_scale))
                    else:
                        uvs.append((p[0] / uv_scale * (-1 if nrm[2] > 0 else 1), p[1] / uv_scale))
        # Re-read loops in final order (normal_flip reverses loops).
        vmap = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(verts)}
        for loop in f.loops:
            loop[self.uv].uv = uvs[vmap[loop.vert]]
        return f

    def quad_strip_uv(self, pts, mat, outward, u0, u1, v0, v1, smooth=False):
        return self.face(pts, mat, outward, uvs=[(u0, v0), (u1, v0), (u1, v1), (u0, v1)], smooth=smooth)

    def box(self, mn, mx, mat, uv_scale=1.0, skip=(), mats=None):
        x0, y0, z0 = mn; x1, y1, z1 = mx
        faces = {
            'top': ([(x0, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z1)], (0, 1, 0)),
            'bottom': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z1), (x0, y0, z1)], (0, -1, 0)),
            'west': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x0, y1, z0), (x0, y1, z1), (x0, y0, z1)], (-1, 0, 0)),
            'east': ([(x1, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z1), (x1, y0, z1)], (1, 0, 0)),
            'south': ([(x0, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x0, y1, z0)], (0, 0, -1)),
            'north': ([(x0, y0, z1), (x1, y0, z1), (x1, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z1)], (0, 0, 1)),
        }
        for k, (pts, n) in faces.items():
            if k in skip:
                continue
            m = mats.get(k, mat) if mats else mat
            self.face(pts, m, n, uv_scale=uv_scale)

    def cylinder(self, c, axis, r, length, mat, seg=16, caps=True, cap_mat=None, smooth=True, r2=None, start_angle=0.0):
        """Cylinder/frustum from c (base centre) along a unit axis ('x','y','z' or vector)."""
        a = {'x': Vector((1, 0, 0)), 'y': Vector((0, 1, 0)), 'z': Vector((0, 0, 1))}.get(axis, None)
        a = Vector(axis).normalized() if a is None else a
        t = Vector((0, 1, 0)) if abs(a.y) < 0.9 else Vector((1, 0, 0))
        u = a.cross(t).normalized(); v = a.cross(u).normalized()
        r2 = r if r2 is None else r2
        c = Vector(c); e = c + a * length
        ring0 = []; ring1 = []
        for i in range(seg):
            ang = start_angle + i / seg * math.tau
            d = u * math.cos(ang) + v * math.sin(ang)
            ring0.append(c + d * r); ring1.append(e + d * r2)
        for i in range(seg):
            j = (i + 1) % seg
            mid = (ring0[i] + ring0[j] + ring1[i] + ring1[j]) / 4
            out = mid - (c + a * (length / 2))
            out = out - a * out.dot(a)
            self.face([tuple(ring0[i]), tuple(ring0[j]), tuple(ring1[j]), tuple(ring1[i])], mat, tuple(out),
                      uvs=[(i / seg, 0), ((i + 1) / seg, 0), ((i + 1) / seg, 1), (i / seg, 1)], smooth=smooth)
        if caps:
            cm = cap_mat or mat
            self.face([tuple(p) for p in ring1], cm, tuple(a), uvs=[(0.5 + 0.5 * math.cos(start_angle + i / seg * math.tau), 0.5 + 0.5 * math.sin(start_angle + i / seg * math.tau)) for i in range(seg)])
            self.face([tuple(p) for p in ring0], cm, tuple(-a), uvs=[(0.5 + 0.5 * math.cos(start_angle + i / seg * math.tau), 0.5 + 0.5 * math.sin(start_angle + i / seg * math.tau)) for i in range(seg)])

    def prism(self, poly, y0, y1, mat, top=True, bottom=False, side_mat=None, uv_scale=1.0):
        """Vertical prism over a convex XZ polygon."""
        cx = sum(p[0] for p in poly) / len(poly); cz = sum(p[1] for p in poly) / len(poly)
        if top:
            self.face([(p[0], y1, p[1]) for p in poly], mat, (0, 1, 0), uv_scale=uv_scale)
        if bottom:
            self.face([(p[0], y0, p[1]) for p in poly], mat, (0, -1, 0), uv_scale=uv_scale)
        for i in range(len(poly)):
            a = poly[i]; b = poly[(i + 1) % len(poly)]
            ex, ez = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
            nx, nz = ez, -ex
            if nx * ((a[0] + b[0]) / 2 - cx) + nz * ((a[1] + b[1]) / 2 - cz) < 0:
                nx, nz = -nx, -nz
            self.face([(a[0], y0, a[1]), (b[0], y0, b[1]), (b[0], y1, b[1]), (a[0], y1, a[1])], side_mat or mat, (nx, 0, nz), uv_scale=uv_scale)

    def rounded_box(self, mn, mx, rad, mat, axis='x', seg=4, mats=None, skip=()):
        """Box with its two top edges along `axis` ('x' or 'z') rounded by `rad`; sides flat.
        Profile is built in the cross-section plane and extruded along the axis."""
        x0, y0, z0 = mn; x1, y1, z1 = mx
        if axis == 'x':
            w0, w1, l0, l1 = z0, z1, x0, x1
        else:
            w0, w1, l0, l1 = x0, x1, z0, z1
        prof = [(w0, y0)]
        for i in range(seg + 1):
            ang = math.pi - i / seg * (math.pi / 2)
            prof.append((w0 + rad + math.cos(ang) * rad, y1 - rad + math.sin(ang) * rad))
        for i in range(seg + 1):
            ang = math.pi / 2 - i / seg * (math.pi / 2)
            prof.append((w1 - rad + math.cos(ang) * rad, y1 - rad + math.sin(ang) * rad))
        prof.append((w1, y0))

        def P(w, y, l):
            return (l, y, w) if axis == 'x' else (w, y, l)
        side = mats.get('side', mat) if mats else mat
        topm = mats.get('top', mat) if mats else mat
        endm = mats.get('end', mat) if mats else mat
        n = len(prof)
        for i in range(n - 1):
            a = prof[i]; b = prof[i + 1]
            mw, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
            cw, cy = (w0 + w1) / 2, y0 + (y1 - y0) * 0.35
            out = (mw - cw, my - cy)
            o3 = P(out[0], out[1], 0)
            o3 = (o3[0], o3[1], o3[2]) if axis == 'x' else o3
            if axis == 'x':
                o3 = (0, out[1], out[0])
            else:
                o3 = (out[0], out[1], 0)
            m = topm if (a[1] >= y1 - rad - 1e-6 and b[1] >= y1 - rad - 1e-6) else side
            self.face([P(a[0], a[1], l0), P(b[0], b[1], l0), P(b[0], b[1], l1), P(a[0], a[1], l1)], m, o3,
                      smooth=(i not in (0, n - 2)))
        if 'end0' not in skip:
            self.face([P(w, y, l0) for (w, y) in prof], endm, (-1, 0, 0) if axis == 'x' else (0, 0, -1))
        if 'end1' not in skip:
            self.face([P(w, y, l1) for (w, y) in prof], endm, (1, 0, 0) if axis == 'x' else (0, 0, 1))
        if 'bottom' not in skip:
            self.face([P(w0, y0, l0), P(w1, y0, l0), P(w1, y0, l1), P(w0, y0, l1)], side, (0, -1, 0))

    def merge(self, dist=1e-5):
        bmesh.ops.remove_doubles(self.bm, verts=self.bm.verts, dist=dist)

    def build(self, collection=None, merge=False):
        if merge:
            self.merge()
        me = bpy.data.meshes.new(self.name)
        self.bm.to_mesh(me)
        self.bm.free()
        for m in self.mats:
            me.materials.append(get_mat(m))
        ob = bpy.data.objects.new(self.name, me)
        (collection or bpy.context.scene.collection).objects.link(ob)
        return ob


def text_mesh(name, body, font_path, size, extrude, mat, origin_unity, right_unity, up_unity, align='CENTER', spacing=1.0):
    """Flat or extruded text: glyph x -> right_unity, glyph y -> up_unity, extrude toward right x up."""
    cu = bpy.data.curves.new(name + 'Curve', 'FONT')
    cu.body = body
    cu.font = bpy.data.fonts.load(font_path)
    cu.size = size
    cu.extrude = extrude
    cu.align_x = align
    cu.align_y = 'BOTTOM'
    cu.space_character = spacing
    tmp = bpy.data.objects.new(name + 'Tmp', cu)
    bpy.context.scene.collection.objects.link(tmp)
    deps = bpy.context.evaluated_depsgraph_get()
    me = bpy.data.meshes.new_from_object(tmp.evaluated_get(deps))
    bpy.data.objects.remove(tmp)
    r = BD(right_unity).normalized(); u = BD(up_unity).normalized(); n = r.cross(u)
    m = Matrix((
        (r.x, u.x, n.x, 0), (r.y, u.y, n.y, 0), (r.z, u.z, n.z, 0), (0, 0, 0, 1)))
    o = B(origin_unity)
    m.translation = o
    me.transform(m)
    if m.to_3x3().determinant() < 0:
        me.flip_normals()
    me.materials.clear(); me.materials.append(get_mat(mat))
    ob = bpy.data.objects.new(name, me)
    bpy.context.scene.collection.objects.link(ob)
    return ob


def rock_wall(mb, a, b, y_top, y_bot, mat, inward_amp=0.28, seg_len=1.6, seg_h=1.8, seed=0.0, flare=None, top_mat=None):
    """Faceted rock face along XZ segment a->b (outward = right-hand side of a->b seen from above, chosen by caller
    passing points CCW around a convex footprint). Vertices move inward only, so the visible rock stays inside the
    collision plane; the top row stays exact. `flare(y)` returns outward growth below the KO plane."""
    ax, az = a; bx, bz = b
    L = math.hypot(bx - ax, bz - az)
    tx, tz = (bx - ax) / L, (bz - az) / L
    nx, nz = tz, -tx  # outward for CCW footprints in Unity XZ (x right, z up)
    nu = max(1, int(round(L / seg_len)))
    nv = max(1, int(round((y_top - y_bot) / seg_h)))
    grid = []
    for j in range(nv + 1):
        y = y_top - (y_top - y_bot) * j / nv
        row = []
        for i in range(nu + 1):
            s = L * i / nu
            px, pz = ax + tx * s, az + tz * s
            if j == 0:
                d = 0.0
            else:
                n1 = noise.noise(Vector((px * 0.45 + seed, y * 0.35, pz * 0.45 - seed)))
                n2 = noise.noise(Vector((px * 1.3 - seed, y * 1.1, pz * 1.3 + seed)))
                d = -inward_amp * (0.55 + 0.45 * n1) - inward_amp * 0.35 * abs(n2)
                if i == 0 or i == nu:
                    d *= 0.35  # keep corners close to the footprint
            if flare is not None:
                d += flare(y)
            row.append((px + nx * d, y, pz + nz * d))
        grid.append(row)
    for j in range(nv):
        for i in range(nu):
            q = [grid[j][i], grid[j][i + 1], grid[j + 1][i + 1], grid[j + 1][i]]
            m = top_mat if (top_mat and j == 0) else mat
            # split into triangles for faceted shading
            mb.face([q[0], q[1], q[2]], m, (nx, 0, nz), uv_scale=8.0)
            mb.face([q[0], q[2], q[3]], m, (nx, 0, nz), uv_scale=8.0)


def export_fbx(path, objects=None):
    if objects is not None:
        for o in bpy.context.scene.objects:
            o.select_set(o in objects)
    bpy.ops.export_scene.fbx(filepath=path, use_selection=objects is not None, object_types={'MESH', 'EMPTY'},
                             apply_unit_scale=True, apply_scale_options='FBX_SCALE_ALL', bake_space_transform=True,
                             axis_forward='-Z', axis_up='Y', mesh_smooth_type='FACE', use_mesh_modifiers=True,
                             add_leaf_bones=False, use_custom_props=False, path_mode='STRIP', embed_textures=False,
                             use_tspace=False)
    print('exported', path, len(bpy.context.scene.objects), 'objects')


def stats():
    tris = 0
    for o in bpy.context.scene.objects:
        if o.type == 'MESH':
            o.data.calc_loop_triangles()
            tris += len(o.data.loop_triangles)
    print('objects', len(bpy.context.scene.objects), 'tris', tris)

For the bottom faces I'm flipping the v coordinate to keep UVs consistent, and now I'm starting a script to build the platform asset, setting up paths and resetting the scene.

I'm defining the footprint polygon for the platform in CCW order and writing an inset function that computes inward-offset edges per side, then intersects adjacent offset lines to find the new chamfered vertices. I'm mapping out which edges correspond to the southwest chamfer, south side, southeast chamfer, east side, and the north gap edge.

Now I'm setting coping widths (wider on the north gap edge), planning the platform top as an inset polygon with slab material, and laying out the coping band geometry with a top face, outer vertical face, and a beveled 45° chamfer at the top edge before transitioning to the rock wall below.

The coping quads share vertices at each corner so there are no gaps between edges. I'm also positioning the yellow safety line just inside the north coping on the slab, and planning placement for three "MIND THE GAP" text instances along that edge.

For snow drifts, I'm generating irregular flat polygons hugging the inset corners along the non-north edges, using noisy inner boundaries to make the drift bands feel natural rather than geometric.

I'm triangulating these as strips of quads between the edge and offset points, making them patchy by driving the width through noise and skipping sections where it drops too thin, with the coping left bare of snow. Then I'm moving to the rock walls around each platform edge, treating the north-facing wall near the gap differently from the rest.

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/laststop/blender')
from lslib import *

reset()
OUT = sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--') + 1]
FONT = '/usr/share/fonts/TTF/DejaVuSansCondensed-Bold.ttf'
KO = -10.0

# Collision footprint listed clockwise in the shell script; CCW here (X right, Z up seen from above).
PLAT = [(-16.0, -9.5), (-13.5, -12.0), (13.5, -12.0), (16.0, -9.5), (16.0, 0.0), (-16.0, 0.0)]
COPING = [0.45, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45, 0.58, 0.45]  # per edge; edge 4 runs along the gap
MASONRY_BOTTOM = -1.7
DEEP = -42.0


def inset(poly, dists):
    n = len(poly)
    lines = []
    for i in range(n):
        a = Vector((poly[i][0], poly[i][1])); b = Vector((poly[(i + 1) % n][0], poly[(i + 1) % n][1]))
        t = (b - a).normalized(); nin = Vector((-t.y, t.x))
        lines.append((a + nin * dists[i], t))
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        (p1, d1), (p2, d2) = lines[i - 1], lines[i]
        den = d1.x * d2.y - d1.y * d2.x
        s = ((p2.x - p1.x) * d2.y - (p2.y - p1.y) * d2.x) / den
        q = p1 + d1 * s
        out.append((q.x, q.y))
    return out


def flare(y):
    return 0.0 if y >= -12.0 else (-12.0 - y) * 0.32


INNER = inset(PLAT, COPING)

# ── Walkable top: slabs inside the coping. ──
top = MB('PlatformSlabs')
top.face([(p[0], 0.0, p[1]) for p in INNER], 'LS_PlatformSlabs', (0, 1, 0), uv_scale=6.0)
top.build()

# ── Coping band with a chamfered outer lip, flush with the collision footprint. ──
cop = MB('PlatformCoping')
n = len(PLAT)
for i in range(n):
    a, b = PLAT[i], PLAT[(i + 1) % n]
    ia, ib = INNER[i], INNER[(i + 1) % n]
    ta = Vector((b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1])).normalized()
    nout = Vector((ta.y, -ta.x))
    ch = 0.07
    a2 = (a[0] - nout.x * ch, a[1] - nout.y * ch); b2 = (b[0] - nout.x * ch, b[1] - nout.y * ch)
    # Pull the chamfer line back along neighbouring edges so corners meet cleanly.
    cop.face([(ia[0], 0, ia[1]), (ib[0], 0, ib[1]), (b2[0], 0, b2[1]), (a2[0], 0, a2[1])], 'LS_Coping', (0, 1, 0), uv_scale=2.0)
    cop.face([(a2[0], 0, a2[1]), (b2[0], 0, b2[1]), (b[0], -ch, b[1]), (a[0], -ch, a[1])], 'LS_Coping', (nout.x, 1, nout.y), uv_scale=2.0)
    cop.face([(a[0], -ch, a[1]), (b[0], -ch, b[1]), (b[0], -0.38, b[1]), (a[0], -0.38, a[1])], 'LS_Coping', (nout.x, 0, nout.y), uv_scale=2.0)
cop.build()

# ── Masonry retaining band, then faceted rock dropping into the clouds. ──
wall = MB('PlatformPillar')
for i in range(n):
    a, b = PLAT[i], PLAT[(i + 1) % n]
    ta = Vector((b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1])).normalized()
    nout = (ta.y, 0, -ta.x)
    wall.face([(a[0], -0.38, a[1]), (b[0], -0.38, b[1]), (b[0], MASONRY_BOTTOM, b[1]), (a[0], MASONRY_BOTTOM, a[1])],
              'LS_Masonry', nout, uv_scale=4.0)
    rock_wall(wall, a, b, MASONRY_BOTTOM, DEEP, 'LS_Granite', inward_amp=0.3, seed=i * 3.1, flare=flare)
wall.build()

# ── Yellow safety line and MIND THE GAP lettering, flush paint on the slabs. ──
paint = MB('PlatformSafetyLine')
z_line0, z_line1 = -0.80, -0.66
paint.face([(-15.3, 0.004, z_line0), (15.3, 0.004, z_line0), (15.3, 0.004, z_line1), (-15.3, 0.004, z_line1)],
           'LS_SafetyYellow', (0, 1, 0))
paint.build()
for k, x in enumerate((-9.6, 0.0, 9.6)):
    text_mesh('MindTheGap%d' % k, 'MIND THE GAP', FONT, 0.62, 0.0, 'LS_SafetyYellow',
              (x, 0.006, -1.52), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), align='CENTER', spacing=1.05)

# ── Flush snow drifts along the outer edges (never on the gap side). ──
snow = MB('PlatformSnowDrifts')
for i in range(n):
    if i == 4:
        continue
    a, b = INNER[i], INNER[(i + 1) % n]
    va, vb = Vector(a), Vector(b)
    L = (vb - va).length
    t = (vb - va).normalized(); nin = Vector((-t.y, t.x))
    steps = max(2, int(L / 0.45))
    prev = None
    for s in range(steps + 1):
        u = s / steps
        p = va.lerp(vb, u)
        w = 0.15 + 0.9 * max(0.0, noise.noise(Vector((p.x * 0.35, p.y * 0.35, i * 1.7))) + 0.15)
        w *= min(1.0, u * 5, (1 - u) * 5) + 0.35
        cur = (p, p + nin * w)
        if prev is not None and (w > 0.2 or prevw > 0.2):
            q = [(prev[0].x, 0.003, prev[0].y), (cur[0].x, 0.003, cur[0].y), (cur[1].x, 0.003, cur[1].y), (prev[1].x, 0.003, prev[1].y)]
            snow.face(q, 'LS_Snow', (0, 1, 0), uv_scale=3.0)
        prev, prevw = cur, w
snow.build()

stats()
export_fbx(OUT)

content.thinking:
I'm worried the snow drift offset of 0.003 above the slab might not be enough to avoid z-fighting at distance, given the near/far plane range of 0.1 to 5000 units reduces depth precision far from the camera.

To be safe, I'll bump up offsets for these decal elements: 0.012 for the safety line, 0.014 for text, and 0.01 for snow, keeping them distinct so they don't overlap each other since they're all small enough to not be noticeable above the collision plane at y=0.

I'm also noticing a potential issue with the coping chamfer geometry — when offsetting a shared vertex along each adjacent edge's own outward normal independently, the chamfer line endpoints for neighboring edges won't coincide at that vertex, which could leave small triangular gaps at the corners.

I'm fixing that by computing a shared inset polygon for all chamfer corners at once, so each edge's chamfer quad and vertical face reference consistent corner points rather than recomputing offsets edge-by-edge. Then I'm working through the math for the text's local coordinate axes — mapping the glyph's right and up vectors into Blender space to figure out which direction the glyph's face normal points, since that determines whether the text reads correctly when viewed from the intended angle.

Verifying the determinant confirms there's no unwanted flip, so the text sits facing up with the correct reading direction. I check the material assignment (just the safety yellow material, no UVs needed since it's a flat color) and note the FBX export will lack UVs but that's acceptable. Now I'm ready to fix the coping and decal offsets and run the export.

The preview renders, though the material colors look desaturated under studio lighting—slabs appear gray rather than beige. The "MIND THE GAP" text reads mirrored from the north-facing view since that's looking at the back of the text, which is expected, while from the south it's too small at that distance to read clearly.

The rock relief facets feel too grid-like and regular; I want to jitter vertex positions along edges and add low-frequency bulges/recesses for more natural variation, keeping displacement inward-only. I'll also detect faces tilting upward after displacement (normal.y > 0.35) and assign them a snow material for occasional ledges. The masonry band and coping look fine as-is, so next I'll refine the shared rock function before checking the platform under real materials in Unity.

The pipeline and platform proportions check out, but the rock relief looks too uniform and grid-like, so I'm reworking `rock_wall` with jittered vertices, low-frequency bulges/recesses, and snow on upward-facing facets.
